    Americans vote in midterms that will determine control of Congress and Trump’s agenda

Summary of midterm results so far

The Democratic party has taken control of Congress in a major setback for Donald Trump and Republicans. Here are some of the key results, historic victories and political developments from the midterm elections so far:

  • The Democrats have secured 228 seats in the House (with 218 needed for a majority) and 54 seats in the Senate (with 51 needed for control). The party has flipped at least seven Senate seats in red states and battlegrounds, including Kansas – which hasn’t elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century – Iowa, Texas, Ohio, Maine, North Carolina and South Carolina. In the House, the Democrats have flipped more than two dozen districts.

  • History was made in Michigan as Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, an Egptian American doctor, became the first Muslim ever elected to the US Senate, beating Republican Mike Rogers for the key battleground seat. “You took a chance on the unlikeliest of candidates,” El-Sayed said in his election night speech.

  • Other seismic wins in federal and state races for the Democrats include James Talarico, who became the first Democrat in 38 years to win a US Senate seat in Texas; Adam Hamilton, who is now the first Democrat to win a US Senate seat in Kansas since 1932; and progressive Troy Jackson, who unseated Susan Collins in Maine, ending her 30-year career in the US Senate.

  • Democrat Aaron Ford won the race for governor in Nevada, toppling Republican incumbent Joe Lombardo and becoming the state’s first black governor.

  • Donald Trump said he was “absolutely willing to accept those results” in an interview with the New York Times. He added: “We’ll, you know, look forward to working with them [Democrats] … We’ll probably work something out.”

  • Former US president Barack Obama has welcomed the midterm election results as a clear rejection of divisive politics. “Tonight, the American people sent a clear message – they want a politics that brings people together rather than divides them, and leaders who offer concrete solutions to the challenges they face,” he said.

Read our full report here:

Fox News host Sean Hannity, one of Donald Trump’s most prominent supporters in conservative media, has acknowledged that the scale of public “hatred” towards the US president contributed to the Republicans’ heavy midtern election losses.

“Hatred is a hell of a motivator,” he told fellow panellist Harold Ford Jr.

He added: “I think the hatred for this man is unprecedented. I’ve never seen anything like it.”

In another historic first, the Democrats are projected to win Nevada’s second congressional district for the first time since its creation in 1981.

Democrat Teresa Benitez-Thompson is in the lead ahead of Republican David Flippo, although the race has not yet been called by the Associated Press.

If she holds on to that lead and flips the House seat, it will mark the first time since 1947 that Nevada has had an all-Democrat congressional delegation. Democrat incumbents have swept all of Nevada’s three remaining House seats, whose races have been called by AP.

“One of the biggest upsets in Nevada history, a district never held by a Democrat in its 45 years of existence,” said Jon Ralston, founder and CEO of the Nevada Independent, of Benitez-Thompson’s projected win.

David Smith

Democrat James Talarico has won the US Senate race in Texas, breaking a 38-year drought for his party in the Republican stronghold and delivering a stunning blow to Donald Trump.

Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton, the state attorney general and a staunch ally of the US president, in one of the most closely watched contests of the midterm elections to decide control of Congress.

“We just took back Texas!” the 37-year-old told jubilant supporters at an election night party in Austin, the state capital and his home city. “We just proved that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas. We have just shown that a politics of division is no match for a politics of love.”

Read more:

Democrat Aaron Ford makes history as Nevada elects its first black governor

Nevada has elected Democrat Aaron Ford as its next governor, making him the first black person to hold the office in the state’s history.

His win toppled the Republican incumbent Joe Lombardo in a closely watched race, and delivered an important victory for the Democrats in one of the country’s key battleground states.

Ford ran his campaign with the backing of California governor Gavin Newsom and former vice-president Kamala Harris, focusing on the cost of living, housing affordability and student debt.

Opinion: The death knell of Trumpism has finally sounded

Moira Donegan

There’s a certain freedom in low expectations. Going in to Tuesday’s midterm elections, forecasts were so grim for the Republicans that poll watchers started trading a kind of knowing joke: that the results would either mean the end of the Trump era, or the end of the polling profession.

Amid those sorts of predictions, any Republican victories would have seemed like a minor miracle. The expectation was that Democrats would have a blowout; Republicans, counting on the final tally to be a bit more mixed, would therefore almost certainly have the freedom to claim that they’d done better than anyone had thought they would.

It will be difficult to credit those spins today. The electorate issued the president a message of dissatisfaction with the second Trump term, and voted decisively to curb his power.

Now, with a Senate majority, Democrats will be able to investigate the president and his cabinet members, draw public attention to their own agenda items, assert Congress’s constitutional prerogatives, and block Republican judicial appointments.

In the coming days and weeks, Trump will alternately say that the Republican losses were fake – the result of fraud by a nefarious but ill-defined conspiracy of Democrats and illegal immigrants – and that they were real, but somebody else’s fault.

His administration has signaled over the past weeks that it could make efforts to contest the certification of especially close Senate races, notably Alaska.

But the wind may have gone out of the sails of that plan for now: for what it’s worth, which isn’t much, Trump told the New York Times on Tuesday night that he would accept the results of the midterms. What’s certain is that he will rail into microphones and complain in all caps on social media. But it is not likely that any of that will go anywhere. Because Tuesday night – almost exactly 10 years after he won the presidency in an upset victory over Hillary Clinton in 2016 – the Trump era effectively came to an end.

Read more:

'The American people sent a clear message,' says Obama

Former US president Barack Obama has welcomed the midterm election results as a clear rejection of divisive politics.

In a statement on X, he said:

Tonight, the American people sent a clear message – they want a politics that brings people together rather than divides them, and leaders who offer concrete solutions to the challenges they face.

These results were only possible because outstanding candidates stepped forward in every region of the country – including in areas once considered long shots. They came from different backgrounds and represented a range of political perspectives, but were united by shared values, a belief in public service, and a commitment to putting the people of their districts and states first.”

Sam Jones

Spain’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez – who has been Donald Trump’s most vociferous European critic – is celebrating last night’s results, hailing them as proof of a progressive fightback and of the “crumbling” of what he called the “ultra wave”.

“Yesterday, the American people voted against policies that only serve to impoverish people,” he posted on X. “Against hate. Against sexism. Against climate denialism and against the privileges of the elites.”

Sánchez, who faces an uphill battle to secure another term in office in Spain’s general election at the end of the month, added: “It happened in Brazil. It just happened in the US. And it will happen soon in Spain.”

Democrat Tina Kotek wins re-election for governor in Oregon

The incumbent Democratic governor of Oregon, Tina Kotek, has won her re-election bid against Republican Christine Drazan.

It is the second time Kotek has defeated Drazan, after the two faced off in the 2022 governor race.

Republican Pete Ricketts wins re-election in Nebraska Senate race

Republican senator Pete Ricketts has won his re-election bid in Nebraska, defeating independent candidate Dan Osborn.

Ricketts, a former Nebraska governor, was appointed to the Senate in 2023 to replace Republican senator Ben Sasse and won a special election in 2024 to serve the final two years of his predecessor’s term.

Taz Ali

History was made in Michigan as Abdul El-Sayed, an Egptian American doctor, became the first Muslim ever elected to the US Senate, beating Mike Rogers for the key battleground seat.

His victory is all the more remarkable given the ugly campaign of anti-Muslim rhetoric that sought to undermine his candidacy, led by Donald Trump and his Republican allies.

The Democrat’s faith was weaponised throughout the race, with Trump calling him a “jihadist” and Rogers questioning his loyalty to the US. El-Sayed met the attacks with defiance, telling Trump that he could “just go on and call me senator after November”.

In his victory speech, El-Sayed told a jubilant crowd:

My name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, and I am so proud and honoured to stand here as your Senator-elect from the great state of Michigan.

Up until right about now, you might have noticed I always say inshallah, or God willing, whenever the outcome of this race was mentioned. But today, tonight, we can turn that inshallah into an alhamdulillah (praise be to God).”

My colleague Joseph Gedeon has more:

Latest midterm results - at a glance

It’s 3am ET in Washington/8am GMT, and as people start seeing their phones ping with notifications, here are where things stand at the moment.

  • Democrats have won control of Congress in a stunning rebuke of Donald Trump’s agenda, delivering an astonishing result and a widely predicted “blue wave” across the country. As of now, Democrats have clinched 54 seats in the Senate (they needed 51 to reclaim the majority) and 225 House seats (they needed 218 to take control of the lower chamber). We’re still awaiting the results for several races – namely in Alaska.

  • There were several seismic and historic wins in federal and state races for Democrats. James Talarico became the first Democrat in 38 years to win a US Senate seat in Texas; Adam Hamilton is now the first Democrat to win a US Senate seat in Kansas since 1932; In Maine, progressive Troy Jackson unseated Susan Collins after a thirty-year grip on the state’s US Senate seat; and Abdul El-Sayed won the US senate race in Michigan – one of the cycle’s most closely watched competitions.

  • We’re waiting on a number of nail-biting races to be called. The race for US Senate in Mississippi is extremely close, and could see a Democratic upset, and it’s still to early to call the Senate contest in Alaska.

  • Democrats also made history in a number of gubernatorial races. Keisha Lance Bottoms’ victory in Georgia means that she will be the first Black female governor in US history. Gina Hinojosa makes history as Texas’ first Latina governor, and the first Democrat to occupy the governor’s mansion since 1990. Meanwhile, David Crowley became Wisconsin’s first Black governor after winning his race tonight.

  • Donald Trump said he was “absolutely willing to accept those results” in an interview with the New York Times. He added: “We’ll, you know, look forward to working with them [Democrats] … We’ll probably work something out.”

item.title: Democrats win control of the House of Representatives (223 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-election/democrats-house-control-midterm-election-wins-trump-check-rcna603397, See on Hacker News

Democrats won control of the House of Representatives with what could be their largest majority in nearly two decades, NBC News projects, as voters delivered a stunning rebuke to President Donald Trump and Republicans.

The House projection is based on an analysis that Democrats will win about 255 House seats — an estimate that could still tick up or down by a few seats but will be well beyond the 218 needed to secure a majority.

NBC News has projected the Democrats will also flip control of the Senate, putting them in charge of both chambers.

Democrats needed to win a net of just three seats to take back the majority. The blue wave washed over many more GOP-held seats than that — from the East Coast to Texas’ Rio Grande Valley — most in districts that Trump carried in 2024.

A quartet of GOP incumbents in Pennsylvania were defeated. Democrat Bob Harvie beat GOP Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, a leader of the bipartisan Problem Solvers Caucus; Democrat Bob Brooks knocked off GOP Rep. Ryan Mackenzie in the 7th Congressional District; Paige Cognetti bested GOP Rep. Rob Bresnahan in the 8th District; and Democrat Janelle Stelson ousted GOP Rep. Scott Perry, a former chairman of the far-right Freedom Caucus, in the 10th District.

In Virginia, Democratic former Rep. Elaine Luria won back her old seat, defeating Republican Rep. Jen Kiggans in the Virginia Beach area, while Democrat Shannon Taylor upset longtime GOP Rep. Rob Wittman outside Richmond.

Another big name in Republican politics, Rep. Tom Kean Jr. of New Jersey, lost his race for re-election to Democrat Rebecca Bennett. Rep. Victoria Spartz, R-Ind., the first Ukrainian-born member of Congress, who frequently clashed with Trump and GOP leaders, also was defeated. And in Colorado, Democratic state Rep. Manny Rutinel trounced GOP Rep. Gabe Evans.

One of the biggest prizes of the night for Democrats was Richard Ojeda II’s upset of Rep. Richard Hudson, R-N.C. As chairman of the House GOP’s campaign arm, Hudson was responsible for protecting GOP incumbents and the majority.

The Democrats’ victory was widely seen as a referendum on Trump’s unpopular policies, including his tough immigration crackdown, the eight-month Iran war and tariffs on U.S. allies that drove up the prices of gas, groceries and other goods.

When the party takes control of the chamber on Jan. 3, it will be the first time in Trump’s second term that he won’t have full control of Congress.

Since he returned to the White House, Trump has tested the limits of his executive powers, dismantling federal agencies through the Department of Government Efficiency, unilaterally imposing sweeping tariffs and rescinding congressionally approved funding — all while the GOP-controlled House and Senate mostly looked the other way.

Follow live updates on the midterm elections

The House Democratic leader, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who barnstormed across the country in the final weeks of the campaign, is expected to make history on Jan. 3 when he is sworn in as the first Black speaker of the House.

He walked into his election night watch party to raucous cheers as the rap song “Unbelievable,” by the Notorious B.I.G., played on the speakers. The midterm results show the “American people are crying out for transformational change,” Jeffries told supporters.

“Today begins the great American comeback. The American people have spoken all across the land, in the North, in the South, in the East, in the West, in the Midwest, from sea to shining sea. The American people have spoken and made clear they’ve had enough of the extremism, enough of the corruption,” Jeffries said at the gathering in Washington.

“They want a Congress that’s going to deliver for the American people,” he said, “and that is exactly what House Democrats will do as soon as we get into office in January.”

With their new majority, Democrats will take control of House committees, gaining subpoena power and the ability to conduct oversight investigations of Trump’s administration, family and business ventures. That could take up considerable time and resources for Trump and his allies, forcing uncomfortable public hearings or prompting legal showdowns over subpoenas.

And in a callback to Trump’s first term, some Democrats have vowed to impeach him for a third time, though there is an internal debate about whether that’s the right political path.

Jeffries told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” that Democrats “haven’t ruled anything in and we haven’t ruled anything out” on impeachment.

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., now poised to become chairman of the powerful Oversight Committee in January, said his panel plans to focus on “Trump family corruption,” including Trump’s cryptocurrency ventures, which have earned him more than $1 billion. The panel will also scrutinize “abuses” by ICE and the Department of Homeland Security, corporate corruption and the Jeffrey Epstein files.

Aside from investigative power, House Democrats will also command the ability to pass legislation with a simple majority. Jeffries has said Democrats would focus on four areas: reversing Trump’s cuts to Medicaid, extending the Affordable Care Act credits, restoring congressional authority related to tariffs and stopping Trump’s war with Iran.

“I wouldn’t characterize it as investigating them like crazy. We’re going to follow the facts, apply the law, be guided by the Constitution and let the chips fall where they may,” Jeffries told reporters at Democrats’ campaign headquarters before the election.

The results are a blow to Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who was launched from obscurity into the top job and has led House Republicans for the past three years. It’s unclear whether Johnson, a close Trump ally, will fight to remain as minority leader or step aside; the latter would trigger a fiercely competitive GOP race to replace him.

House Democrats had the political wind at their backs; they needed to flip a net of just three seats to win back the majority they lost in 2022. And Trump’s dismal approval rating was a major factor in the GOP’s loss.

Historically, the president’s party tends to lose seats in midterm elections. Only in two midterms in the modern era did a party buck that trend — in 1998, when voters punished Republicans for impeaching President Bill Clinton, and in 2002, as President George W. Bush rallied support in the wake of the 9/11 terrorist attacks.

Still, the battle for House control played out primarily on GOP turf this cycle, with Democrats already holding 215 seats, including a dozen in battleground districts. On top of that, results of this cycle’s mid-decade redistricting wars ended up favoring Republicans slightly, though Democrats quickly moved to neutralize what could have been a large GOP advantage.

Trump fired the first shot in the summer of 2025, when he urged GOP allies in Texas to redraw their congressional lines to help the party pick up as many as five seats. Republicans also redrew maps in places like Florida, North Carolina, Tennessee, Alabama, Louisiana and Missouri in a bid to win more seats.

But Democrats countered in California, with Gov. Gavin Newsom, former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and their allies successfully rallying support for Proposition 50, which approved a new congressional map drawn by state Democrats. That map helped Democrats pick up GOP-held seats.

While the GOP successfully picked up a handful of majority-Black, Democratic-held seats in the South, the Supreme Court blocked Missouri Republicans’ new congressional map, essentially preserving the Kansas City seat of longtime Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver.

“We made a promise to aggressively push back against the MAGA extremist effort to rip the election away from the American people by gerrymandering the possibility of Democrats winning the majority out of existence,” Jeffries said before the election, adding that the redistricting wars will continue in the 120th Congress.

“This fight is not over; we’ve just gotten started,” he added. “It will continue into the next Congress until we pass legislation signed into law by a future president that will prohibit mid-decade gerrymandering from ever happening again.”

item.title: Distinct cellular and genetic differences in colorectal cancer in young patients (117 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.dana-farber.org/newsroom/news-releases/2026/study-reveals-distinct-cellular-and-genetic-differences-in-colorectal-cancer-in-younger-patients, See on Hacker News

Researchers identified age-associated differences in tumor composition and gene activity, creating a foundation for investigating why colorectal cancer can be more aggressive in younger adults

Dana-Farber Cancer Institute researchers, along with Mass General Brigham researchers from the Gene Lay Institute of Immunology and Inflammation, and the Broad Institute, have uncovered biological clues to why colorectal cancer can behave more aggressively in younger people. Published today in Nature Medicine, the study — the largest of its kind — lays a foundation for understanding age-associated differences in colorectal cancer and exploring future treatments.

In the United States, colorectal cancer diagnosis rates among people younger than 50 rose 2.9% per year from 2013 through 2022, according to the American Cancer Society. Its 2026 report identifies colorectal cancer as the leading cause of cancer death in this age group. Younger patients are also more likely to be diagnosed at advanced stages, underscoring the need to better understand the biology of early-onset disease.

"Through Dana-Farber’s Young-Onset Colorectal Cancer Center, we see how profoundly this disease can affect younger patients and their families, often during the busiest and most formative years of life," said co-senior author Kimmie Ng, MD, MPH, who is the director of the Young-Onset Colorectal Cancer Center at Dana-Farber. "This collaborative work with Mass General Brigham researchers from the Gene Lay Institute and researchers from the Broad Institute gives us important new insight into the biology of these tumors. The findings provide a valuable roadmap for further investigating the distinct features of young-onset colorectal cancer. Our ultimate goal is to discover novel strategies for prevention, diagnosis, and treatment for our young patients."

"The need to understand why colorectal cancer is affecting younger adults at increasing rates is urgent," said co-senior author Ana C. Anderson, PhD, a core faculty member of the Gene Lay Institute of Immunology and Inflammation at Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Massachusetts General Hospital, and Harvard Medical School. "And that starts with understanding the biology of the disease across the entire lifespan. By looking beyond conventional age cutoffs, we’ve uncovered biological patterns that earlier studies may have missed and created a foundation for the field to investigate them further. While we’re still at the beginning of understanding what these differences mean, our work gives researchers a new direction to pursue in tackling this urgent problem in human disease."

The research team, led by first author Caroline Porter, PhD, of the Klarman Cell Observatory at the Broad Institute, studied specimens from surgeries stored in Dana-Farber’s Gastrointestinal Biobank from surgeries at Brigham and Women’s Hospital. Co-senior authors include Anderson, Ng, and Ramnik J. Xavier, MD, PhD, of the Broad Institute, Mass General Brigham, and the Gene Lay Institute. They analyzed 189 tumors from patients ages 29 to 90+, including 54 diagnosed before age 50, and 135 diagnosed at age 50 or older. Using a technique called single-nucleus RNA sequencing, the researchers measured gene activity in more than 850,000 cancer cells and other cells in the tumors. The technique, which works with frozen tissue, enabled the team to build a detailed map of tumor cells by studying archived samples with extensive clinical record data.

Rather than dividing the tumor samples into two data sets and comparing the younger and older age groups, the researchers looked for factors that changed gradually with age, accounting for tumor location, stage, sex, and prior treatment in their analyses. This approach revealed subtle differences that likely would have been obscured by a simple two-data set comparison.

Among tumors of the most common colorectal cancer subtype, younger patients’ tumors had a significantly higher proportion of connective and supporting cells relative to cancer cells. A higher proportion of connective and supporting cells has been linked to chemotherapy resistance in several types of solid cancer. The team confirmed this pattern using gene-activity data from 564 other tumors and computer analysis of stained tissue images from another 712 tumors. 

Younger patients also had higher activity of long non-coding RNAs, molecules that can regulate genes without making proteins. Some appeared repeatedly across different types of cancer cells. Many are "dark" RNAs, whose functions remain largely unknown. The team also saw gene activity suggesting stronger signaling between cells that can help cancer cells move and invade nearby tissue in younger patients.

"Our study is an advance from previous work in that we analyzed tumors from a large number of patients and used single-cell approaches to find novel features unique to tumors from young patients," said Xavier, a co-senior author of the study, a core institute member at the Broad Institute, Kurt Isselbacher Professor at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School, and Vice Director of the Gene Lay Institute. Xavier is also a gastroenterologist at Mass General Brigham. "This work sets the stage for future mechanistic studies on how these cell programs interact with chemicals from the diet and from gut microbes to cause early-onset colorectal cancer." 

Although the findings provide key insight into colorectal cancer in young individuals, they do not yet provide proof that these differences cause more aggressive disease. One remaining question is whether there are differences in immune responses in these tumors across ages — the researchers' methods captured relatively few immune cells. Future studies will explore how these changes may affect cancer growth and spread, and whether they offer opportunities for prevention or treatment.

Authorship: Authors include Caroline B. M. Porter, Shane P. Murphy, Jules Cazaubiel, Toni M. Delorey, Liat Amir-Zilberstein, Orr Ashenberg, Liubou Klindziuk, Elizabeth Andrews, William Tan, Kosuke Matsuda, Atsushi Kondo, Satoko Ugai, Tomotaka Ugai, Shuji Ogino, Emily Finan, Jacques Deguine, Ewa Sicinska, Lauren K. Brais, Jennifer S. Thalappillil, Marios Giannakis, Ramnik J. Xavier, Ana C. Anderson and Kimmie Ng.

Disclosures: Anderson is a member of the scientific advisory boards for Compass Therapeutics, Zumutor Biologics and Cytospire; these interests were reviewed and managed by Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Mass General Brigham in accordance with their conflict-of-interest policies. Ogino has served as a consultant for Sanofi Pasteur. Xavier is a co-founder of Convergence Bio, a scientific advisory board member at Nestlé and Magnet BioMedicine, and a board director at MoonLake Immunotherapeutics; these organizations had no role in the study. Deguine is a member of BioRender’s scientific advisory board. Giannakis receives institutional research funding from Janssen and Sunbird Bio, has consulted for Nerviano Medical Sciences, and has received honoraria from OncLive and PER. Ng consults for or serves on advisory boards for Bayer, Pfizer, CytomX, Jazz Pharmaceuticals, Revolution Medicines, Agenus, Johnson & Johnson, AbbVie, Sanofi, GlaxoSmithKline, Flagship Pioneering, AstraZeneca, Amgen, CRICO and Manta Cares; receives institutional research funding from Pharmavite and Janssen; and serves as an Associate Editor at JAMA. Her interests were reviewed and managed by Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in accordance with its conflict-of-interest policies.

Funding: This study was funded in part by the Gene Lay Institute of Immunology and Inflammation, Helen Gurley Brown Foundation/Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Project P Fund, Patrick Beauregard Fund, Poorvu-Jaffe Fund for Young-Onset Colorectal Cancer Research, The Thau Fund, the Eigner Fund for Young-Onset Colorectal Cancer, the Klarman Cell Observatory at Broad Institute, National Institutes of Health (R01 CA205406, P30 DK043351, R01 CA285851, P01 CA87969, UM1 CA186107, P01 CA55075, UM1 CA167552, U01 CA167552, R01 CA151993, R35 CA197735), and the American Cancer Society Clinical Research Professor Award (CRP-24-1185864-01-PROF).

item.title: C++26 Disapproved (390 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://andreasfertig.com/blog/2026/11/cpp26-dis-failed-how-does-cpp-survive/, See on Hacker News

On October 23, 2026, the unthinkable happened. It was supposed to be a mere formality: C++26 was up for a vote by the ISO National Bodies (NBs). The options are always approval, rejection, or abstention. Comments are also allowed. Since 1998, this process had run quietly and smoothly. Not so on October 23, 2026. After a twelve-week voting period, the result is in: Disapproved!

I would like to mention here that I am a member of the C++ Standardization Committee and, together with my colleagues, represent Germany’s vote. ISO rules also stipulate that certain votes are internal to ISO, and the results—or the breakdown of the results—may not be published. This article contains my own personal views.

The Current Status

As far as I know, this is the first time in the history of C++ that DIS ballot failed. When I searched the ISO system, I could only find one other DIS that was not approved: ISO/IEC DIS 26926 C++/CLI Language Specification dated August 11, 2006. It’s possible that my search privileges aren’t sufficient to view everything, but all ISO programming languages should be visible to me. The sad end of ISO/IEC DIS 26926: the project was halted. I mention this upfront to clarify the significance of this vote.

In the following, I will use various terms from everyday ISO terminology. At https://isocpp.org/std/iso-iec-jtc1-procedures, there is an overview of the various stages of an ISO standard. DIS is the penultimate stage. As the overview also shows, a two-thirds majority is required. This majority was not achieved.

The reason for the rejection is quite clear from the comments submitted by the National Bodies (NBs): contracts. Put simply, a number of NBs believe that this feature is not yet ready for release.

The Process

Now it gets complicated. The C++ Standardization Committee, also known as WG21, follows ISO rules but also has some additional rules. One of these is (or was) that opinions are always heard whenever new information becomes available. If an opinion was heard and a feature was nevertheless not changed as desired, the person respects the outcome and accepts that many others disagree.

However, the voting body at the NB level may also consist of other individuals, or the NBs are, of course, free to vote differently.

The previous practice was that NBs would only vote against a standard if new information became available or if errors in the process or similar issues were identified. This changed on October 23, 2026.

It’s difficult to judge in this complex situation; the NBs who want C++26 without Contracts argue that there is new information. I myself find it hard to share this view. A new paper with old arguments is not new information to me.

The History of Contracts in C++

The feature has been on the wish list for a long time. I was already in the room in Cologne back in 2019, at the time for C++20, when Contracts, in a different form back then, were being included in the standard. I was also in the room when the feature was removed from C++20 again during the same meeting. As a result, a study group was formed to address the topic of Contracts and its various aspects from 2020 to approximately 2024. Afterward, the study group submitted its work and proposals to the Evolution Working Group (EWG), the central body for language extensions. There, the topic was discussed further over several meetings before being included in C++26 by a majority vote.

In the next step, WG21 voted on the C++26 draft in March 2026, which included Contracts. Here, too, a large majority was achieved, though not without dissenting votes.

And that brings us to the next phase: DIS. At this stage, there were enough “no” votes that a two-thirds majority was not reached.

What happens next?

The big problem: what happens next? ISO, of course, has a process for this. It offers various options:

  1. Submit a revised draft for a new DIS vote.
  2. Submit a revised draft to the committee (that would be the CD phase).
  3. Publish a revised draft as a Technical Specification.
  4. Cancel the project.

All of these possibilities mean a delay in the next C++ standard. Whether it will still be called C++26 is also up in the air, but that’s a much smaller issue.

The difficulty with all four options is that they require a majority within WG21. However, this working group voted to move C++26 with Contracts into the next voting phase leading to its release. And it did so with more than just the required two-thirds majority. The feature didn’t come out of nowhere, either; it was developed over the course of years through the work and possibly personal commitment of many people. It’s hard to imagine that this group would simply want to abandon its work, which has received approval on multiple occasions so far. The same applies to the group that is dissatisfied with Contracts. This group, too, has invested effort, in some cases even in alternative implementations. It’s hard to imagine that, after these groups voted “no” in the DIS vote, the result would change without Contracts being removed.

Even the last option removing C++26 requires a majority in WG21. As I understand it, this step would mean reverting to C++23 and proceeding to C++29 without a single change. This would affect the work of even more people. WG21 would then be tasked with incorporating features that have already been successfully included in C++26 into C++29. Since this can only be done through a paper backed by at least one person advocating for it, features could be omitted if that person lacks the motivation or time.

Of course, certainty about the voting outcome can only be achieved if the respective path is actually taken.

Unfortunately, the way forward is currently more than uncertain. Perhaps this also explains why ISO/IEC DIS 26926 marked the end of this activity. Consensus is needed to move forward. Trust is always required for consensus. Unfortunately, that trust has just been shaken.

The next C++ standard, and thus the future of C++, is currently at an impasse.

The good news is that the next meeting will take place on November 16, which is just a few days away. The top priority will be to break the deadlock. This will very likely have implications for C++29 as well; in fact, there is currently no reason to continue working on this project.

My Personal Opinion

Normally, my articles are technically focused and free of personal opinion. Regarding the rejected DIS, I can only say that I consider it a massive disaster and feel sorry for the entire C++ community. Regardless of whether someone likes Contracts, considers them important, or sees major weaknesses in them, the topic has been worked on for years and has received a majority vote multiple times in its current form. By voting “no,” an established system, one based primarily on trust and respectful collaboration, has been shaken. Every ISO standard is simply a set of compromises. Everyone loses sometimes, and everyone wins sometimes. Overall, the result is one in which all participants have given their best. During the DIS vote, the losing parties refused to accept their loss. The question that primarily determines how to move forward is whether the group can rebuild trust.

Andreas

item.title: The Internals of PostgreSQL (336 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.interdb.jp/pg/index.html, See on Hacker News

I am officially open to new international opportunities! 🌍

After a temporary stay in Japan to focus on my health and personal responsibilities, I am fully recovered, ready, and excited to work abroad again.

I am highly interested in returning to Europe, as well as opportunities in the Southern Hemisphere and Southeast Asia.

Looking for:

  • Challenging tasks in PostgreSQL.
  • Roles offering international visa sponsorship OR Remote work that supports a digital nomad lifestyle.

If your team is hiring, let’s connect! Please feel free to reach out via e-Mail(hironobu @ interdb.jp or interdb.mx @ gmail.com) or DM.

What’s New
  • 26 Sep 2026: 11th Anniversary! This content was launched on 26 September 2015.
  • 28 Jun 2026: Section 8.5, “Asynchronous I/O in PostgreSQL” Published.
  • 1 May 2026: Chapter 12, “Logical Replication” (Beta Version) Published.
  • 14 Dec 2024: Added Conflicts in Section 11.2.4.

The Internals of PostgreSQL

PostgreSQL is a well-designed, open-source multi-purpose relational database system which is widely used throughout the world.

It is one huge system with the integrated subsystems, each of which has a particular complex feature and works cooperatively with each other. Although understanding of the internal mechanism is crucial for both administration and integration using PostgreSQL, its hugeness and complexity make it difficult.

The main purposes of this documentation are to explain how each subsystem works, and to provide the whole picture of PostgreSQL.

This documentation covers versions 19-beta (excluding the new buffer page lock mechanism) and earlier.

Some academic papers have referred to this documentation. The Chinese version of this documentation was published in June 2019.

This documentation was first published on 26 September 2015.

Contents

  • Chapter 1. Database Cluster, Databases and Tables
  • Chapter 2. Process and Memory Architecture
  • Chapter 3. Query Processing
  • Chapter 4. Foreign Data Wrappers (FDW)
  • Chapter 5. Concurrency Control
  • Chapter 6. VACUUM Processing
  • Chapter 7. Heap Only Tuple (HOT) and Index-Only Scans
  • Chapter 8. Buffer Manager
  • Chapter 9. Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)
  • Chapter 10. Online Backup and Point-In-Time Recovery (PITR)
  • Chapter 11. Streaming Replication
  • Chapter 12. Logical Replication (Beta Version)
Hironobu SUZUKI

I am a software programmer/engineer, the author of:

  • The Internals of PostgreSQL
  • The Engineer’s Guide To Deep Learning
  • pg_plan_inspector
  • pg_tuner

I graduated from graduate school in information engineering (M.S. in Information Engineering), have worked for several companies as a software developer and technical manager/director. I published seven books in the fields of database and system integration (4 PostgreSQL books and 3 MySQL books). In June 2019, the Chinese book of this documentation was published.

As a director of the Japan PostgreSQL Users Group (2010-2016), I organized the largest (non-commercial) technical seminar/lecture on PostgreSQL in Japan for more than six years, and also served as the program committee chair of the Japan PostgreSQL Conference in 2013 and as a member in 2008 and 2009.

In June 2022, my interview article was published in “PostgreSQL person of the week”.

Cuando era joven, vivió en Sudamérica por unos años. Recientemente, a veces vuelve a allí.

I am seeking a remote position focused on the application of ML and AI technologies to DBMS. For personal reasons, I will be living in Japan for several years.

      Blog

Contact

Please read the following FAQ before sending messages.

Since publishing my content, I’ve been fortunate to receive a lot of positive feedback, which is truly gratifying. However, unfortunately, I’ve encountered individuals in the past who tried to misuse my content for self-promotion 1.

These experiences have shaped the approach I’ve outlined below.

  1. Who can use this documentation freely?
    If you are a teacher or a student belonging to an educational organization, you can freely use this documentation and figures in your study. Anyone can use this documentation and figures with noncommercial meetings and lectures, if you state the link to this site and the copyright; otherwise, contact me.
  2. Is it available for commercial contents?
    This content can be used under two options:
    There was a comment on Hacker News that took this seriously, but of course, it’s a joke. To be clear, I have no intention of having any commercial ties to this. Regardless, you can imagine the kind of requests I get on a daily basis.
    • Revenue Share: You can leverage this content after a revenue share agreement is signed. Under this agreement, you’ll share 20% of the sales generated from using this content.
    • Full Buyout: In very rare cases, I consider requests for full commercial use of all content on this site. For a complete buyout of all content rights, the cost is €5,000,000.
  3. Does the author need any help to write?
    No. I am writing for my own enjoyment. Even if you send me your article, I will never include it in my documentation.
  4. Why doesn’t the author use the GitBook or other e-book formats/sites?
    I am using the best tools I need and I will decide what I use. I am always trying a lot of tools for better explanations.
    Simply put, this documentation is optimized to read on html file and it is hard to convert to other formats.
    I do not have any plan to make PDF version and Smartphone versions because of same reason.
  5. Why doesn’t the author use RSS to notify the update?
    I keep my domain and my server to provide my documentation; you can read when you want to read. What do you want more?
  6. Why doesn’t the author waive the copyright of this documentation or use the creative commons license?
    I’d like to ask you what problems you have by that I keep on having the copyright of my documentation.

After reading, send a message to my twitter in public.

or  

If you use email, please provide at least two SNS addresses (e.g. LinkedIn, Twitter) for verification purposes. Due to the XZ backdoor incident, I no longer accept contact from anonymous individuals.

Copyright

© Copyright ALL Right Reserved, Hironobu SUZUKI.

For any inquiries regarding the use of this documentation or any of its figures, please contact me.

Exception Educational institutions can use this documentation freely.

View PDF HTML (experimental)

Abstract:This book provides a compact, derivation-oriented introduction to the mathematical foundations of modern generative artificial intelligence. Rather than surveying every recent architecture or implementation detail, it develops a coherent route through the ideas connecting major families of generative models, from PCA, probabilistic PCA, variational autoencoders, and diffusion models to normalising flows, autoregressive factorisations, GANs, Wasserstein GANs, and energy-based models. The aim is to make the structure of generative modelling more accessible without removing the mathematical substance needed to understand how these models are derived and related. The book is intended as a foundation-building primer for mathematically curious researchers, practitioners, and students.

item.title: Safari introduces Adaptive Dark Mode in 27.3 (485 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://webkit.org/blog/18541/introducing-adaptive-dark-mode/, See on Hacker News

We’re excited to announce Adaptive Dark Mode in Safari 27.3 beta. When enabled by a user, Safari adapts light websites and presents them as dark.

In the spring of 2019, Safari 12.1 became the first browser to support dark mode on the web. A lot of people love using dark mode, but not every website has a dark version. Almost 40% of web page loads are from users in dark mode, and yet only 10% of page loads support it. If you love dark mode, you’ve probably hit a site that felt particularly bright. Adaptive Dark Mode is designed to close that gap, providing a consistent dark experience across the web.

You can try it today in Safari 27.3 beta. To enable, first make sure your system appearance is set to dark. Then browse to a website with a bright background. Safari will offer a preview of Adaptive Dark Mode. Tap ‘Try’.

For websites that signal support of dark mode with <meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark"> in HTML or color-scheme: light dark in CSS, Adaptive Dark Mode does not change a thing. For the rest of the web, it quickly analyzes the page, looking at colors and estimating whether it’s predominantly light or dark. If the page generally has a dark background with light text, nothing is changed. When a page has a light appearance, Adaptive Dark Mode adapts the page to be dark.

How does Adaptive Dark Mode work?

At the core of Adaptive Dark Mode is the transformation of color. Sometimes colors are simply decorative, while other times they have semantic meaning. Adaptive Dark Mode determines when to invert colors so elements remain visible or when to leave colors unchanged.

While creating Adaptive Dark Mode, we developed a color matrix to invert the luminosity of colors while preserving hue. It’s used to make light backgrounds dark, and dark text light. When transforming text color, Adaptive Dark Mode aims for sufficient contrast as defined by the WCAG 4.5:1 contrast ratio. Light CSS gradients are also transformed to dark.

Adaptive Dark Mode makes careful judgments so transformed content looks good and stays usable: buttons have contrast against backgrounds, text is visible over images, and hover menus look clear.

It takes the same care with images. Most are left unchanged, preserving their integrity. But many icons and logos can lose contrast when the background color behind them is inverted. So Adaptive Dark Mode inspects SVG images and transforms colors when needed. For bitmap images, it analyzes the pixel histograms and inverts simple black-and-white logos.

Effects like masks and mix-blend-mode can create undesirable results on an element whose colors have been transformed, so in some cases Adaptive Dark Mode turns such effects off. Also, <canvas> content is left unchanged, since canvases contain a wide range of content that’s hard to predict.

It’s precisely because Adaptive Dark Mode is happening deep within the WebKit browser engine that we are able to find creative ways to solve the most complex challenges, apply the transformations with great speed and power efficiency, all while rigorously protecting user privacy.

Making your site work even better

In general, a web page will work well with Adaptive Dark Mode if it follows good modern web development practices.

If your site still uses older techniques, small updates can help. For logos and icons, swap bitmap images for SVG. Use solid or gradient colors in CSS instead of tiled background images. Replace image sprites with modern CSS for rounded corners, shadows, and button states. Create content images with transparent backgrounds instead of baking the page background color into the image. Add padding to containers to prevent crowding.

Perhaps you want a specific dark mode experience for a certain portion of the page. Apply color-scheme: light dark to the relevant element and add your own dark styles.

Building your own dark mode

For complete control over how your site looks in dark mode, add full support. It’s a terrific time to do so. It’s never been easier.

All the web technology needed to fully support dark mode is widely available today, including:

  • <meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark">
  • :root { color-scheme: light dark }
  • @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { }
  • <picture><source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)">
  • light-dark()

Newer CSS functions like color-mix() and contrast-color(), plus popular techniques for organizing design systems with CSS variables provide additional options and flexibility.

Be sure to declare dark mode support using the color-scheme meta tag in your HTML head and/or by setting the color-scheme property on :root or body in your CSS. Don’t wait to inject this information later via JavaScript. This best practice helps ensure your site is rendered correctly as fast as possible.

Using the “light only” color scheme

If you would like your web app or website to not be transformed by Adaptive Dark Mode, you can communicate this using color-scheme. The HTML <meta name="color-scheme" content="light only"> tag lets browsers know that 1) this page supports light mode and 2) should only be displayed in light mode. The color-scheme: light only rule does the same thing, but with the flexibility of CSS, allowing you to just target specific elements on the page — or of course, you can target the whole page with :root { }. (Note: the ‘only’ keyword is not supported in Safari 27.3 beta 1. Check back as Adaptive Dark Mode evolves through the beta process.)

Protecting user privacy

Apple firmly believes user privacy is a fundamental human right. If websites could detect when a user has enabled Adaptive Dark Mode, that would increase the amount of fingerprintable information and weaken privacy protections against trackers.

As a result, Safari prevents websites from detecting when Adaptive Dark Mode has been applied. JavaScript that queries CSS colors will get the original authored colors, not the transformed ones. Any images drawn into canvas render in their original form.

Feedback

If you manage a website or web app, and would like to discuss how Adaptive Dark Mode is adapting your project, feel free to reach out at web-evangelist@apple.com.

If you try out Adaptive Dark Mode as a user, and find a site that does not work well, we’d love for you to file a report with Feedback Assistant. (Learn more about filing Feedback).
