item.title: I dumped Apple’s word list (160 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://helgesver.re/articles/macos-vulgar-word-flags, See on Hacker News

I Dumped Apple's Fucking Word List

November 3, 2026

TL;DR

  • ~/Library/Keyboard/VulgarWordUsage.db is real. It records which swear words you use, per app and per recipient, so autocorrect learns to stop "ducking" you. On my Mac it is empty, and typing swear words into a native app did not fill it.
  • The interesting part is upstream. Apple's system dictionary flags every word with one of three tiers (vulgar, offensive, sensitive) and up to eleven topic flags (sex, drugs, religion, politics, violence, …).
  • There is no public API for any of it. I read the flags with a few private C functions from Lexicon.framework. Code below, in C and in Swift. The full dumps for 15 languages are in this gist (uncensored, so mind the content warning).
  • Highlights: Oedipus is vulgar. Tom and Mick are offensive. pee, poo, niggle and underling are sensitive. And "Trump" is the only living politician in the English sensitive tier, next to Hitler, Mao, Osama bin Laden and the Taliban. Biden, Obama and Putin are clean.

Content note: this article prints the words uncensored, slurs included, because the whole point is to see what Apple flags. The one exception is the n-word: it is in the list in English and several other languages, and I'm not writing it out.

It started with a tweet

Nick posted this, I asked where it lives, and he answered. A database that tracks my profanity is not something I can leave alone, so I opened mine.

The database

$ sqlite3 -readonly ~/Library/Keyboard/VulgarWordUsage.db .schema
CREATE TABLE properties (ROWID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, key, value, UNIQUE (key));
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "vword_usage" (
    ROWID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    app                          TEXT, -- app identifier
    recipient                    TEXT, -- recipient identifier
    vword                        TEXT, -- vulgar word
    word_reading                 TEXT, -- the reading form of a word (relevant for Japanese)
    usage_count                  INTEGER DEFAULT 0,
    last_use_timestamp           REAL DEFAULT 0, -- last use timestamp (seconds since the reference date)
    journaled
);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX app_recipient_vword_word_reading_idx ON vword_usage(app, recipient, vword, word_reading);

So the keyboard can know that you say fuck in Messages to one particular friend, but not in Mail to your boss. The unique index is on (app, recipient, word, reading), so that is the granularity.

Mine has zero rows. The properties table holds version = 2 and nothing else. The file was last written in April 2024.

What it is for

At WWDC in June 2023, Craig Federighi announced the iOS 17 autocorrect rewrite with this line: "In those moments where you just want to type a ducking word, well, the keyboard will learn it, too." (TechCrunch, NPR)

This database is how it learns. The symbol names in the macOS shared library cache spell out the flow:

TI::VulgarWordUsageDatabaseWrapper::set_current_app_id(CFString)
TI::VulgarWordUsageDatabaseWrapper::set_current_recipient_ids(vector<string>)
TI::VulgarWordUsageDatabaseWrapper::increment_usage_count(word, reading, recipients)
TI::VulgarWordUsageDatabaseWrapper::decrement_usage_count(...)
TI::VulgarWordUsageDatabaseWrapper::can_autocorrect(word, app, recipients)
TI::VulgarWordUsageDatabaseWrapper::can_autocorrect_somewhere(word, reading)
KB::FilterNonVulgarIfTopCandidateVulgar::filter_candidates(...)
KB::Candidate::every_vulgar_word_is_allowlisted(VulgarWordUsageDatabaseWrapper*, ...)

Plus log strings like Passing recipient IDs to the vulgar word usage database wrapper; number of IDs: %lu.

In plain terms:

  1. When you start typing, the keyboard engine tells the wrapper which app you're in and who you're writing to.
  2. When you type a vulgar word and keep it, its count goes up for that app and those recipients. Undoing the word brings the count back down.
  3. When the engine ranks suggestions, it asks whether every vulgar word in a candidate is allowlisted for this context. If it isn't, the clean alternative wins: ducking.

A _KSUserWordsSynchroniser sharedAcrossLanguagesVulgarWordUsageValue symbol suggests it syncs between devices like your other learned words.

Mine is empty

I tried to fill it. Using agent-desktop, I opened a new TextEdit document and typed well fuck this shit, damn it., first as a text insert, then as individual key presses. Nothing changed: no row, no log line, and the file's modification date stayed in 2024.

I don't know why, and I couldn't work it out. Maybe the Mac never records anything here, or maybe it only does so in some apps or settings. If you've got rows in yours, tell me what you did.

That would be a short article. But the database only counts words that are already known to be vulgar. So who decides that?

Where the word list lives

Searching the dyld shared cache for "vulgar" turned up a C API with an LX prefix (LXVulgarWordUsageDatabaseCreate, LXVulgarWordUsageDatabaseCanAutocorrect, …) and, more usefully, two functions on dictionary entries:

_LXEntryGetCategoryFlags
_LXEntryGetMetaFlags

LX is Lexicon.framework, a private framework that reads the per-language dictionaries under /System/Library/LinguisticData/. Every word in those dictionaries is an LXEntry with two 32-bit flag fields. If the vulgarity rating is anywhere, it's in those bits.

There is no public API

I looked. NSSpellChecker, UITextChecker, NaturalLanguage and UILexicon don't expose vulgarity. SensitiveContentAnalysis covers images and video, not text. The only places "profanity" shows up on developer.apple.com are App Store age ratings and review guidelines.

So: private functions. Lexicon has no headers, but the C functions are exported, and their signatures are easy to guess because they follow CoreFoundation conventions. This program opens the dictionary for a locale, walks every entry, and prints both flag fields:

// lx.c — dump every word in a system lexicon with its flags.
// clang -O1 -o lx lx.c -F/System/Library/PrivateFrameworks -framework Lexicon -framework CoreFoundation
#include <CoreFoundation/CoreFoundation.h>
#include <stdbool.h>
#include <stdio.h>

typedef const void *LXLexiconRef, *LXCursorRef, *LXEntryRef;
extern CFStringRef kLXLexiconLocaleKey;
LXLexiconRef LXLexiconCreate(CFDictionaryRef options, CFErrorRef *error);
LXCursorRef  LXLexiconCreateRootCursor(LXLexiconRef);
void         LXCursorEnumerateEntriesRecursively(LXCursorRef, void (^)(LXEntryRef, bool *stop));
CFStringRef  LXEntryCopyString(LXEntryRef);
uint32_t     LXEntryGetCategoryFlags(LXEntryRef);
uint32_t     LXEntryGetMetaFlags(LXEntryRef);

int main(int argc, char **argv) {
  CFStringRef locale = CFStringCreateWithCString(NULL, argc > 1 ? argv[1] : "en_US", kCFStringEncodingUTF8);
  const void *keys[] = {kLXLexiconLocaleKey}, *values[] = {locale};
  CFDictionaryRef options = CFDictionaryCreate(NULL, keys, values, 1, &kCFTypeDictionaryKeyCallBacks,
                                               &kCFTypeDictionaryValueCallBacks);
  LXLexiconRef lexicon = LXLexiconCreate(options, NULL);
  if (!lexicon) return 1;

  LXCursorEnumerateEntriesRecursively(LXLexiconCreateRootCursor(lexicon), ^(LXEntryRef entry, bool *stop) {
    char word[512] = "";
    CFStringRef s = LXEntryCopyString(entry);
    if (s) { CFStringGetCString(s, word, sizeof word, kCFStringEncodingUTF8); CFRelease(s); }
    printf("%08x\t%08x\t%s\n", LXEntryGetCategoryFlags(entry), LXEntryGetMetaFlags(entry), word);
  });
}

$ ./lx en_US | wc -l
  199019
$ ./lx en_US | awk -F'\t' '$3 == "fuck" || $3 == "table" || $3 == "Trump"'
00000000	00800002	fuck
00000000	00000000	table
00002000	02000081	Trump

The same thing in Swift, loading the functions at runtime with dlopen and dlsym so you don't need to link against a private framework. It prints only words that carry one of the three tiers:

// lexflags.swift — swiftc -O lexflags.swift -o lexflags && ./lexflags en_US
import Foundation

let lexicon = dlopen("/System/Library/PrivateFrameworks/Lexicon.framework/Lexicon", RTLD_NOW)!
func sym<T>(_ name: String, as _: T.Type) -> T { unsafeBitCast(dlsym(lexicon, name)!, to: T.self) }

typealias LXRef = UnsafeRawPointer
let create     = sym("LXLexiconCreate", as: (@convention(c) (CFDictionary, UnsafeMutablePointer<Unmanaged<CFError>?>?) -> LXRef?).self)
let rootCursor = sym("LXLexiconCreateRootCursor", as: (@convention(c) (LXRef) -> LXRef?).self)
let enumerate  = sym("LXCursorEnumerateEntriesRecursively", as: (@convention(c) (LXRef, @convention(block) (LXRef, UnsafeMutablePointer<Bool>) -> Void) -> Void).self)
let copyString = sym("LXEntryCopyString", as: (@convention(c) (LXRef) -> Unmanaged<CFString>?).self)
let metaFlags  = sym("LXEntryGetMetaFlags", as: (@convention(c) (LXRef) -> UInt32).self)
let category   = sym("LXEntryGetCategoryFlags", as: (@convention(c) (LXRef) -> UInt32).self)
let localeKey  = dlsym(lexicon, "kLXLexiconLocaleKey")!.load(as: CFString.self)

let locale = CommandLine.arguments.dropFirst().first ?? "en_US"
guard let lex = create([localeKey: locale] as CFDictionary, nil), let root = rootCursor(lex) else {
    fatalError("could not open lexicon for \(locale)")
}

let tiers: [(UInt32, String)] = [(0x0080_0000, "vulgar"), (0x0100_0000, "offensive"), (0x0200_0000, "sensitive")]
enumerate(root) { entry, _ in
    let meta = metaFlags(entry)
    guard let tier = tiers.first(where: { meta & $0.0 != 0 })?.1,
          let word = copyString(entry)?.takeRetainedValue() else { return }
    print(tier, String(format: "%05x", category(entry)), word, separator: "\t")
}

Both are read-only. They open the same dictionary the keyboard uses and print it.

Decoding the bits

Apple doesn't document these flags, so every meaning below is inferred: I grouped words by bit and read samples until each group's theme was obvious. The system code helps with one of them. An enum case called offensiveVulgarSensitive sits right next to the vulgar-word code, and three adjacent meta bits match it.

The three tiers (meta flags)

BitTieren_US wordsExamples
0x00800000vulgar1,050fuck, shit, cunt, cock, crap, wtf, fml, bullshitting, fucktard, shizzle, merde
0x01000000offensive663kike, wop, dago, fag, Paki, japs, Klansman, retard, Oriental, ass, asshole
0x02000000sensitive2,558damn, bitch, idiot, LSD, abortion, gun, suicide, anus, pee, poo

In en_US a word has at most one tier: they never overlap. Out of 199,019 entries, 4,271 have one.

Roughly: vulgar is swearing and sex slang, offensive is slurs aimed at groups of people, and sensitive is everything a keyboard shouldn't offer you unprompted: mild swears, insults, drugs, weapons, extremism, disease and bodily functions.

The topics (category flags)

The other field is a topic bitmask, and a word can have several topics:

BitTopicen_US wordsExamples
0x00100excretion123feces, barf, crapper, piddle, pooped
0x00200body parts958nipples, navel, buttock, perineum, triceps
0x00400insults, identity-loaded823idiot, cretin, hick, pleb, sexist, homophobic, blacklist
0x00800disease93Covid, herpes, PTSD, leprosy, monkeypox
0x01000drugs222heroin, shroom, crackhead, hotbox, OD
0x02000politics, extremism266Hamas, Goebbels, Leninism, democrat, swastikas, Trump
0x04000religion, damnation420Sikhism, jihadi, Beelzebub, damn, hell, jeez
0x08000sex473nude, nookie, lecher, harlots, Pornhub, Hooters
0x10000violence, death373suicide, lynch, murders, hangings, slave, slaveholder
0x20000weapons, terrorism268AK-47, grenadier, jihad, sarin, kamikaze, yellowcake
0x40000catch-all "sensitive context"1,080God, Allah, Jews, gay, trans, bi, crazy, fat, ugly, sex, die

The topic flags and the tiers are independent. 2,052 English words have a topic but no tier: gay, fat, God, Allah and sex are all tagged "sensitive context" but are not vulgar, offensive or sensitive. My guess is the topic is a hint ("be careful how you rank this") and the tier is the rule.

The lower meta bits are dull: proper nouns, abbreviations, camel-case brand names like iMac and tvOS. Nothing to see there.

The weird ones

This is where it gets fun. Some flags are obviously right, and some made me laugh.

Vulgar

  • Oedipus: vulgar. Presumably because of motherfucker-adjacent jokes, or the complex. Sophocles would be thrilled.
  • reams: vulgar. As in "to ream someone".
  • cooties: vulgar. Your nine-year-old is swearing.
  • orgy, sext, merde: fair enough.

Offensive

  • Tom and Mick: offensive. Uncle Tom and the slur for Irish people, but also very common first names.
  • Oriental: offensive.
  • papooses: offensive.
  • conservatards: offensive, the one political insult I found in the slur tier.
  • niggardly: offensive. It means "stingy" and comes from Old Norse, unrelated to the slur. It has also caused real controversies, which is presumably why it's there.
  • ass and asshole: offensive, not vulgar.

Sensitive

  • pee and poo: sensitive, with the excretion topic. So are premenstrual, leprosy and herpesvirus.
  • niggle (a small worry, of Scandinavian origin) and underling (Old English for a subordinate) are sensitive and share the insult topic. Similar words aren't flagged: snigger is clean but niggle is flagged, and minion, lackey, flunky and stooge are clean but underling is flagged. These look like hand-picked entries, not rules.
  • blacklist and whitelist are sensitive with the insult/identity topic. That matches the industry move to blocklist and allowlist. Apple's own phrase-filter files are named blocklist.dat.
  • Braves and Chiefs (team names with Native American mascots), Londonderry (the contested name for Derry), Gentile, Jehovah, Mongol and Frenchier are all sensitive.
  • Isis is sensitive with the politics topic. Sorry to the Egyptian goddess.
  • slave, slavery and slaveholder are sensitive with the violence topic.
  • idiot is sensitive in English. Norwegian is stricter and puts idiot in the offensive tier.

The Trump flag

The sensitive tier has 109 capitalized words. Here is all of it:

Al-Qaeda, Al-Qaida, Aryan, Aryans, Auschwitz, Bacchus, Beelzebub, Birkenau, Brave(s), Buchenwald, Chief(s), Chippendale(s), Christ-y, Christer(s), Crip(s), Dachau, Eichmann, Frenchier, Gentile(s), Gestapo(s), Goebbels, Goering, Hamas, Hezbollah, Himmler, Hitler, Hitlerian, Hitlerism, Hitlerite(s), Hitlerjugend, Hooters, Isis, Islamophobe(s), Islamophobic, Jehovah(s), Jewfro(s), Jezebel(s), Kalashnikov(s), Kristallnacht, Kuomintang, Londonderry, Luftwaffe, Mao, Mauthausen, Mickie(s), Mollie(s), Mongol(s), Mossad, Nazi(s), Nazism, Osama, Pornhub, Quaalude(s), Reich, Reichsmark, Reichstag, Sachsenhausen, Satan, Satanism, Shoah, Sinophobe(s), Sinophobic, Sodom, Stasi, Taliban, Treblinka, Trump, Trumps, Unabomber, Uzi(s)

(Plurals and possessives folded for brevity.)

Every other real person on that list is dead, and nearly all of them are Nazi officials, dictators or terrorists. Then there's Trump:

category  meta      word
00002000  02000081  Trump        sensitive tier + politics topic
00002000  02000081  Trumps
00002000  02000081  Trump's
00000000  00000000  trump        (the card-game word: clean)
00000000  00000000  trumped

For comparison:

Worden_US
Trumpsensitive, politics topic
Hitlersensitive, politics topic
Bidenclean
Obamaclean
Putinclean
Stalinclean
Musknot in the dictionary

en_GB matches en_US. Other languages differ: the German dictionary has Trump clean (and puts Hitler in the offensive tier), and Swedish is the one that flags Putin as sensitive.

What the flag does matters here. As far as I can tell, a sensitive word is one the keyboard shouldn't suggest on its own. You can still type it and it won't be corrected away. Think "keep this out of the QuickType bar unless the user is clearly heading there", which is a lot milder than a ban.

There is a plausible reason Apple would want that for one specific name. In February 2025, iPhone dictation briefly showed "Trump" when people said "racist". It went viral, and Apple called it a "phonetic overlap" in the speech model and shipped a fix within a day (9to5Mac). The dictionary files on my Mac are from July 2025. A rule that keeps the name out of unprompted suggestions would stop that kind of thing from happening again through the keyboard. I can't prove that's why it's there, and I don't have an older dictionary to compare against. But it fits.

Norwegian politics, for comparison

Because I'm Norwegian and had to check:

WordTopicTier
FrP, Høyre, Venstre, Rødt, SV, KrF, MDGpoliticsnone
Størepoliticsnone
Solberg, Erna, Sylvinonenone
Listhaugn/anot in the dictionary
Breivik, Quisling, Hitlernonesensitive

Every party gets the politics topic and none gets a tier. The only Norwegians in the sensitive tier are a mass murderer and a Nazi collaborator.

Other languages

The same three tiers exist in every European dictionary I tried, Cyrillic included. The counts are entries, not lemmas, so heavily inflected languages like Polish and Russian look much worse than they are: every case and conjugation of a swear word is a separate entry.

LocaleVulgarOffensiveSensitiveNotable
en_US1,0506632,558idiot is sensitive
en_GB1,0558722,337chav is offensive; chink is filed as vulgar, not offensive
nb_NO2,3931,3246,446idiot is offensive
da_DK1,1793,3148,551fjols ("fool") is offensive
sv_SE6371,24716,193idiot is vulgar; Putin is sensitive
fi_FI56987247The entire sensitive tier is kakka ("poop"), kakkakasa ("pile of poop") and saakeli
de_DE3,2183,5189,446Hitler and beknackt ("daft") are offensive; Trump is clean
nl_NL571,1803,805Only 57 vulgar words, but kanker ("cancer", the classic Dutch swear) is one
fr_FR2,1512625,562boche is offensive
es_ES3,93131313,431sudacas and fachas are offensive
it_IT3,8863776,543terrone is offensive, and so is nazismi
pt_BR1,5901,8913,332machista and velhinhos ("little old people") are offensive
pl_PL9,6981,4366,190The biggest vulgar tier here, mostly inflections (dupczysz, srasz)
ru_RU10,8213,23924,721Same story: мат inflects a lot

The bits don't seem to mean the same thing everywhere. Arabic and Hebrew return hundreds of thousands of "sensitive" entries, so those dictionaries probably reuse the bits for something else, and I left them out. Korean, Catalan and Hungarian return nothing, and Japanese crashes my dumper.

Samples from Norwegian, since that's what I type in when I'm not typing English:

  • Vulgar: faen, jævla, dritt, fitte, kuk, pule, pissehull, rævhull, pulekanin, kåt, morrabrød.
  • Offensive: idiot, sigøyner, kinamann, riskokers (literally "rice cookers", a slur for Asians), plus the Norwegian n-word.
  • Sensitive: helvete, satan, homo, quisling, Breivik, skinhead, abortnekt, trusene ("the panties").

The tier words are mostly what you'd expect, but the edges are different in each language, and that is where the human-edited parts show. Norwegian calls idiot offensive and English calls it sensitive. German thinks Hitler is a slur.

Phrases, not just words

There is a second, separate filter. Every English language model has a blocklist.bundle, and there's a qp_blocklist.bundle for QuickPath, the swipe keyboard:

/System/Library/LinguisticData/RequiredAssets_en.bundle/AssetData/en.lm/
├── blocklist.bundle/{blocklist.dat, blocklistidmap.dat}
└── qp_blocklist.bundle/{blocklist.dat, blocklistidmap.dat}

blocklistidmap.dat is a 20-byte header followed by (lexicon token ID, class ID) pairs of 32-bit integers. Mapping the token IDs back through the dictionary gives 2,544 words in 930 classes. Most classes are inflection groups:

931   fuck | fucked | fucking | fucks
1181  molest | molestation | molested | molester | molesting
1514  died | dies | dying
1611  Holocaust | holocaust | holocausts
1614  denied | denies | deny | denying
923   Semite | Semites | Semitic
1487  ghetto | ghettoes | ghettos
1720  animals | brown | cats

blocklist.dat is a packed trie over those class IDs, so it blocks sequences: "deny" followed by "Holocaust", and whatever 1720 pairs with. A class that puts brown next to animals and cats suggests the list targets specific phrasings rather than single words, though which phrasings I can't tell without decoding the trie. The runtime check is LMLanguageModelTokenSequenceIsBlocklisted in LanguageModeling.framework. I got far enough to learn that its fourth and fifth arguments include an output pointer, but my probe still crashes intermittently, so I haven't read the actual phrases yet. That's for a follow-up.

Caveats

  • Meanings are inferred. Apple documents none of these bits. The tier names come from an enum in the system code and the topics from reading thousands of samples. Both are consistent, but they're still a reading.
  • Flagged is not censored. As far as I can tell these flags decide what the keyboard volunteers, not what you can type.
  • One machine. Everything here comes from macOS 15.6 (24G84) with LinguisticData build 438 from July 2025. iOS and other macOS versions may ship different dictionaries.
  • Private API. The functions can change or disappear in any update. Don't ship this in an app.

Try it yourself

# Your own learned-swears database (probably empty on a Mac)
sqlite3 -readonly ~/Library/Keyboard/VulgarWordUsage.db 'select * from vword_usage'

# Build the Swift version from above and filter by tier
swiftc -O lexflags.swift -o lexflags
./lexflags en_US | awk -F'\t' '$1 == "vulgar" {print $3}' | sort -u | less
./lexflags nb_NO | awk -F'\t' '$3 == "faen" || $3 == "helvete" || $3 == "idiot"'

If you'd rather not build anything, the gist has every tiered word for 15 locales as TSV, plus the code and a script that regenerates them. It's a snapshot of macOS 15.6 and won't be kept up to date.

If you find something funnier than Oedipus, I want to hear about it.

item.title: Preparing for the Flipper One Kickstarter and opening pre-orders (222 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://flipper.net/pages/flipper-one, See on Hacker News

Open Linux computer based on a powerful ARM processor. Network multi-tool — built-in Wi-Fi 6E and Gigabit Ethernet. Expandable via M.2 modules: 5G cellular modem, SDR radio and more.

PRE-ORDER NOW

Follow progress at the Developer Portal >>

OPEN LINUX PLATFORM

Flipper One runs on completely open-source Linux firmware with a mainline kernel. This means ultimate compatibility with bleeding-edge kernel versions, free from vendor-specific BSP limitations and binary blobs. Our goal is to create a fully upstream-supported ARM computer that never becomes outdated, and a well-documented platform giving the community maximum freedom to customize:

  • Full mainline Linux kernel support
  • No binary blobs
  • No vendor-locked BSP

We have partnered with the Collabora team, who are actively working on bringing the RK3576 SoC into the mainline kernel, to make Flipper One fully upstream-supported and free from binary blobs. Read Collabora blog post

CO-PROCESSOR ARCHITECTURE

Two independent processors work together in parallel, each controlling different sub-systems of Flipper One.
This architecture allows you to control the Linux sub-system directly from the built-in LCD display, without losing access to the device even when the Linux kernel is not yet ready or turned off.

Why 2 processors?

  • Low-power MCU (Raspberry Pi RP2350) — an energy-efficient microcontroller responsible for core device control. It drives the LCD display, physical buttons, and status LEDs. It manages the power sub-system and controls the Linux OS boot parameters when the Linux sub-system is off. More about MCU Firmware >>
  • High-performance CPU (Rockchip RK3576) — a powerful 8-core ARM system-on-chip that runs the Linux operating system. It executes user applications, controls all networking interfaces such as Wi-Fi and Ethernet, and manages high-speed peripherals including USB3 and PCIe. It also integrates an NPU for AI acceleration and a GPU for graphics output via HDMI and DisplayPort. More about Linux sub-system >>

ONE CABLE FOR EVERYTHING

Get SSH access and charge the device via a single USB cable! No extra adapters needed for Linux console access or powering the device — Flipper One can simultaneously emulate a virtual network adapter, a serial adapter (COM port), and a mass-storage device.

No drivers required on macOS, Linux, Windows, iOS, or Android.

NETWORK SCANNER

Analyze wired and wireless IP networks. Flipper One helps you map network topology, discover active hosts, and scan for open ports and services. It can also act as a passive sensor to detect network attacks and report anomalies.

POWER METER

The power consumption meter works like a wattmeter, showing in real time how much power the entire system uses, including the CPU and peripherals. It helps you understand what is happening under the hood: whether the system is idle or actively working.

M.2 MODULES

The core idea of Flipper One is an expandable hardware platform. Create your own specialized tool with a high-speed M.2 expansion module that installs inside the device, under the back plate. It supports almost any type of module — cellular or satellite modems, SDR modules, AI accelerators, SSDs (NVMe or SATA), and Wi-Fi cards via adapters.

M.2 tech specs

  • M.2 type: Key-B
  • Supported sizes: 2230 (via extender), 2242, 3042, 3052
  • Supported thickness: up to D3 (double-sided modules)
  • Interfaces: PCIe 2.1 ×1 / USB 2.0 / USB 3.1 / SATA3 / SIM card + eSIM
  • Extra interfaces: Serial Audio / UART / I²C

Open source mounting system

All mechanical parts for module mounting are completely open source. You can design your own antennas, cooling system, and mounting solutions for additional accessories.

GPIO MODULES

DIY modules can be connected via the GPIO connector using standard 2.54 mm pin headers. To make the assembled device easier to carry around, the GPIO module is positioned along the device body and can be covered with a protective cover.

Check out GPIO technical specification and examples of GPIO modules.

Desktop Mode

Connect Flipper One to an external display with a single USB-C cable for a full desktop experience. Support for DisplayPort Alt Mode allows one cable to deliver power, transmit video, and connect USB peripherals such as a keyboard and mouse simultaneously.

Satellite NTN Modem

Satellite modem

NTN (Non-Terrestrial Networks) — is a satellite communication technology, a low-speed connection designed for IoT devices, standardized by 3GPP as part of the 5G and LTE specifications. It uses the standard cellular stack, including SIM/eSIM authentication, roaming, and regular IP traffic.

We want to add NTN satellite connectivity support to Flipper One to help popularize this technology and give engineers and enthusiasts a chance to work with real satellite infrastructure.
To make this happen, we're looking for a partner company like Skylo that's ready to work with us to add support for their satellite network to our eSIM module and help us choose a specific NTN M.2 module that we can officially support.
Read more on the Modules → Satellite modem page.

Built-in Advanced Wi-Fi Chip

Built-in Wi-Fi Chip

We want to build the most versatile integrated Wi-Fi into Flipper One — it needs to support all the features required for Wi-Fi network analysis, including monitor mode and packet injection. For now, we've settled on the popular Mediatek MT7921U chipset. It's modern enough, supports three frequency bands, and ticks just about every box. We're actively testing this chip right now and we'd love you to join in.

Why MT7921AUN?

The same chipset is used in the popular ALFA AWUS036AXML adapter, and there's a sizeable community around the open-source MT7921U driver. The main strengths of this chipset:

  • Modern Wi-Fi 6E: 802.11ax, 2x2 MIMO
  • Frequencies: 2.4 / 5 / 6 GHz bands
  • Open mainline Linux driver: mt7921u
  • Monitor mode support
  • Integrated Bluetooth 5.2

BUILT-IN eSIM

Flipper One has a built-in eSIM chip that comes pre‑provisioned with a Flipper SIM data plan.

To use the eSIM data plan, you need to install a 5G modem in the M.2 slot. You can also switch between the built-in eSIM and a physical SIM card.

What is Flipper SIM?

We're working on an experimental connectivity project for network geeks. Flipper SIM is a universal SIM card for routers, phones, and IoT devices, with advanced features such as always-on connectivity, outage-proof, traffic filtering, and network management tools. We'll share more details soon!

Coming soon

Tech Specs

item.title: macOS 27 does not support CoreStorage volumes (136 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://wadetregaskis.com/macos-27-golden-gate-does-not-actually-support-corestorage-or-hfs-volumes/, See on Hacker News

macOS 15 Sequoia had a hard time with CoreStorage – and thus encrypted HFS+ volumes – since it deprecated both technologies and callously crippled some important tools for working with them, but nonetheless it mostly still worked. While I’d often – but not always – have to manually unlock one of my HFS+ volumes – but not the others – at boot, and it also refused to convert some – but not all – volumes from HFS+ to APFS1, keeping me trapped in the situation – it ultimately still worked. I could get at my data and use the volumes more or less normally.

Unfortunately, in macOS 27 that’s no longer the case. Not only does Golden Gate just not support CoreStorage / encrypted HFS+ volumes, out of the box you can’t do anything with them – can’t mount them, can’t convert them to APFS, can’t even erase them. It renders your expensive storage hardware completely useless.

Worse, macOS 27 puts up a misleading dialog, upon boot, saying that macOS 28 (the next version) won’t support these volumes. I have no idea what Apple’s doing or thinking. Maybe it’s all just an embarrassing misunderstanding – the file system team told the notifications team that CoreStorage & encrypted HFS+ support is going away, and typoed the version number as 28 rather than 27?

Details

macOS 27 cannot mount CoreStorage volumes automatically or through any normal means. Worse, Disk Utility can’t mount them even when manually told to – it just fails with the cryptic error:

com.apple.DiskManagement.disenter error 49,153

diskutil mount also fails, this time with an error message that is a blatant lie:

disk27 is a CoreStorage Logical Volume which is locked; use "diskutil coreStorage unlockVolume"

$ diskutil cs unlockVolume BC304645-7D99-481E-931F-855B3011D89D
BC304645-7D99-481E-931F-855B3011D89D is already unlocked and is attached as disk27
$ diskutil cs list                                             
CoreStorage logical volume groups (1 found)
|
+-- Logical Volume Group 0DC0EFB1-23CC-45BC-B37D-C1BBEBDAFCEB
    =========================================================
    Name:         Smash
    Status:       Online
    Size:         2000054960128 B (2.0 TB)
    Free Space:   0 B (0 B)
    |
    +-< Physical Volume 1B5A1754-184B-4F17-A797-BF69B4BB627F
    |   ----------------------------------------------------
    |   Index:    0
    |   Disk:     disk10s2
    |   Status:   Online
    |   Size:     2000054960128 B (2.0 TB)
    |
    +-> Logical Volume Family 376204CD-8048-4962-B05C-72F4FC16B77B
        ----------------------------------------------------------
        Encryption Type:         AES-XTS
        Encryption Status:       Unlocked
        Conversion Status:       Complete
        High Level Queries:      Fully Secure
        |                        Passphrase Required
        |                        Accepts New Users
        |                        Has Visible Users
        |                        Has Volume Key
        |
        +-> Logical Volume BC304645-7D99-481E-931F-855B3011D89D
            ---------------------------------------------------
            Disk:                  disk27
            Status:                Online
            Size (Total):          1999702634496 B (2.0 TB)
            Revertible:            No
            LV Name:               Smash
            Volume Name:           Smash
            Content Hint:          Apple_HFS

Tangentially: surprisingly, hfsutils (installed via brew) don’t work at all:

$ sudo hmount /dev/disk27
hmount: /dev/disk27: not a Macintosh HFS volume (Invalid argument)
$ sudo hmount /dev/disk10s2
hmount: /dev/disk10s2: not a Macintosh HFS volume (Invalid argument)

But what’s even worse about this dumpster fire is that macOS 27 can mount these volumes just fine – it’s just that all the normal ways to do it are completely broken. If you go down to a lower level and run mount_hfs directly, it does work:

$ sudo mkdir -p /Volumes/Smash
$ sudo mount_hfs -o rdonly /dev/disk27 /Volumes/Smash
$ ls /Volumes/Smash
Documents           Pictures           Scratch space

That said… that -o rdonly parameter… in principle it shouldn’t be required, but I could not get macOS 27 to let me mount any HFS-on-CoreStorage volume as read-write – no matter what I did, it always fails with error “Resource busy” (EBUSY). I spent a lot of time trying to debug this, and could find no evidence of anything having the volume in question open (nothing in lsof etc).

But wait, it gets worse.

macOS 27 can’t even erase the volume. All the normal tools – diskutil, Disk Utility, etc – fail with that same “Resource busy” error.

Workaround

Thankfully, with the help of Gemini 4 Argon, I did find a workaround. It’s convoluted, but takes only a few steps, thankfully.

First, while if you try to delete the logical volume group it ostensibly fails, it doesn’t completely fail – it does actually delete the logical volume(s) within:

$ diskutil cs delete 0DC0EFB1-23CC-45BC-B37D-C1BBEBDAFCEB
Started CoreStorage operation
Unmounting Logical Volumes
Destroying Logical Volume Group
Erasing disk10s2
newfs_hfs: cannot create filesystem on /dev/rdisk10s2: Resource busy
Mounting disk
Could not mount disk10s2 after erase
Error: -69832: File system formatter failed
1 💣 $ diskutil cs list                                       
CoreStorage logical volume groups (1 found)
|
+-- Logical Volume Group 0DC0EFB1-23CC-45BC-B37D-C1BBEBDAFCEB
    =========================================================
    Name:         Smash
    Status:       Offline
    Size:         2000054960128 B (2.0 TB)
    Free Space:   -none-
    |
    +-< Physical Volume 1B5A1754-184B-4F17-A797-BF69B4BB627F
        ----------------------------------------------------
        (No properties)
$ diskutil cs delete 0DC0EFB1-23CC-45BC-B37D-C1BBEBDAFCEB
Started CoreStorage operation
Destroying Logical Volume Group
Error: -69783: Unable to delete the CoreStorage Logical Volume Group

You still can’t destroy it completely, nor can you erase the physical volume yet – the “Resource busy” errors persist. But, the trick is to restart – after that, you can then erase the volume.

So it seems that whatever broken thing is holding the physical volume (or logical volume group) in a ‘busy’ state is tied to the existence of the logical volume(s) therein, and once they’re deleted (and the machine rebooted) the bug stops being triggered.

Call for better workarounds

I’ve glossed over a lot of debugging and attempts I made to save the volume in-place, by either making it work as-is (even if only with e.g. hfsutils) or by converting it to APFS, but neither I nor Gemini 4 Argon could find anything that worked. It’s too late for me – I was forced to just delete all my HFS+ & CoreStorage volumes and rebuild them painstakingly from backups – but if anyone finds a way, I’d love to amend this post, for the benefit of future readers.
